echoes.note: Jesus' catalog of signs answers John by weaving Isaiah's vision of the redeemed: 'the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped' — 'the blind receive sight, the deaf hear' borrows verbatim imagery, marking the dawning kingdom.
'Then shall the lame man leap as a hart' directly underlies 'the lame walk'; Isaiah 35 is the controlling subtext for Jesus' reply, signaling that the eschatological restoration has arrived.

'to preach good news to the poor' (anointed Servant) supplies the climactic 'the poor have good news preached to them' — the same verb/theme Jesus claims as his own programmatic mission (cf. Luke 4:18).
'the dead are raised up' echoes Isaiah's resurrection hope, 'Your dead shall live... the earth shall give birth to the dead,' folded into the kingdom-signs list.
'In that day shall the deaf hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind shall see' — a parallel Isaianic oracle reinforcing the deaf/blind reversal, part of a recurring Isaianic cluster.
The Servant 'to open the blind eyes' resonates with restoring sight; strengthens the Servant-mission reading of Jesus' self-presentation.
'Hear, you deaf; and look, you blind, that you may see' — further Isaianic deaf/blind language drawn into the answer to John.
'the lepers are cleansed' presumes the Torah cleansing rite for the healed leper; the only OT framework for leprosy cleansing, evoked figurally as fulfilled.
Naaman's cleansing is the paradigmatic prophetic leprosy healing; a faint precedent for 'lepers are cleansed' as a sign of prophetic power.

'Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you' is a formula citation ('of whom it is written') of Mal 3:1, 'Behold, I send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before me,' identifying John as the eschatological forerunner.

'Behold, I send a messenger before you' (LXX wording 'before your face') is conflated with Mal 3:1 in the citation; the second-person 'before your face' tracks Exodus more closely than Malachi's 'before me.'
'this is Elijah, who is to come' directly invokes Mal 4:5, 'I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of the LORD,' interpreting John as the returning Elijah.
The Elijah identification draws on the whole Elijah cycle; the wilderness/mantle prophet of austere dress stands behind the contrast with 'soft clothing' and the desert setting.
Elijah 'a hairy man, with a leather belt' grounds the John-as-Elijah figure and the contrast with kingly 'soft clothing'; cf. Matthew's own description of John's garb.
'What did you go out into the wilderness to see?' evokes the wilderness-voice preparing the way, the same way-preparation motif as the Mal 3:1 citation.
'born of women' as a marker of mortal human descent is biblical idiom (cf. Job 14:1; 15:14; 25:4); the phrase frames John as the greatest of mortals.
'Man who is born of a woman is of few days' supplies the idiom 'born of women' for finite humanity, against which John's greatness and the kingdom's superiority are measured.
'wisdom is justified by her children' personifies Wisdom as in Proverbs 8, where Lady Wisdom calls and her children/sons heed her; Jesus and John are vindicated as Wisdom's offspring.
'Wisdom exalts her sons and lays hold of those who seek her' — Second Temple Wisdom personification standing directly behind 'wisdom is justified by her children.'
'a time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance' faintly underlies the children's complaint about piping/dancing and mourning/lament.
Wisdom's banquet invitation supports the wider Wisdom-vindicated theme; contested as a specific source.
The oracle against Tyre (and Sidon, v.4) is the prophetic backdrop for naming Tyre/Sidon as proverbially judged Gentile cities now declared less culpable than the unrepentant Galilean towns.
Ezekiel's extended judgment on Tyre ('I am against you, O Tyre') makes Tyre the type of a doomed city; invoked to shame Chorazin and Bethsaida.
'Set your face against Sidon' — the companion oracle completing the Tyre/Sidon judgment pair Jesus names.
Sodom's fiery overthrow is the archetypal divine judgment; 'more tolerable for the land of Sodom on the day of judgment' presupposes Genesis 19 as the benchmark of destroyed wickedness.
'You, Capernaum, exalted to heaven, you will go down to Hades' reworks the taunt against Babylon's king: 'I will ascend into heaven... yet you shall be brought down to Sheol' (Isa 14:13-15).
'brought down to Sheol' is the direct verbal pattern behind 'go down to Hades'; the proud-exaltation-then-abasement form is borrowed wholesale.
Ezekiel compares Jerusalem unfavorably to Sodom ('Sodom your sister has not done as you'), the same rhetorical move — guilty Israel worse than proverbial Sodom — Jesus makes against Capernaum.
'the punishment of my people is greater than the punishment of Sodom' parallels the comparative-judgment logic; contested as direct source.
'repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes' echoes Nineveh's repentance in sackcloth and ashes, the model Gentile-repentance the Galilean towns failed to match.
Sodom and Gomorrah's overthrow as covenant-curse paradigm reinforces 'the land of Sodom' as judgment shorthand.

'I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth' echoes Daniel's blessing of the God who 'gives wisdom to the wise' yet reveals hidden things — the same revelation-to-the-lowly, concealment-from-the-wise pattern.
'I thank you... you have given me wisdom... made known to us the king's matter' supplies the thanksgiving-for-revelation form behind Jesus' prayer.
'the wisdom of their wise men shall perish' grounds the reversal in which God hides 'these things from the wise and understanding' — the same Isaianic critique of human wisdom.

Sirach 51 opens 'I will give thanks to you, O Lord and King' — a sage's thanksgiving immediately preceding the Wisdom-yoke invitation (Sir 51:23ff) that Matthew 11:28-30 reworks; the thanksgiving + invitation sequence parallels Matthew's.
'What is his name, and what is his son's name?' faintly anticipates the exclusive Father-Son mutual knowing of v.27; contested.
The righteous one 'calls himself a child of the Lord' and claims knowledge of God, a Second Temple anticipation of the Son's unique knowledge of the Father.

Wisdom's invitation 'Draw near to me, you who are untaught... Put your neck under the yoke, and let your souls receive instruction' is the closest analogue: 'Come to me... Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me.' Jesus speaks as incarnate Wisdom issuing her summons.

'Put your neck under her yoke, and let your soul receive instruction... See with your eyes how I have labored little and found for myself much rest' — supplies yoke + labor + rest in the same cluster Jesus uses.
'I have labored little and found for myself great rest' lies directly behind 'I will give you rest' / 'rest for your souls' joined to taking up the yoke.
'ask for the old paths... and you will find rest for your souls' is verbatim behind 'you will find rest for your souls' (Mt 11:29); Jesus offers the rest Jeremiah's generation refused.
'Put your feet into her fetters, and your neck into her collar/yoke... at last you will find her rest' — Sirach's earlier Wisdom-yoke passage doubling the yoke-and-rest motif.
'at last you will find the rest she gives, and she will be changed into joy for you' reinforces the Wisdom-yoke-rest pattern adopted in vv.28-30.
'My presence will go with you, and I will give you rest' is the foundational divine promise of rest; 'I will give you rest' assumes God as the giver of rest.
'gentle and lowly in heart' echoes the humble/meek king who comes 'lowly and riding on a donkey' (Mt 21:5 cites it); the same praus self-description.
'the man Moses was very meek, above all men' offers a precedent for 'I am gentle (meek) and lowly,' figuring Jesus as a new Moses giving an easy yoke.
'his yoke shall depart... his burden depart from off their shoulder' — the relief-from-yoke/burden imagery faintly contrasts with Jesus' light yoke and easy burden.
'Come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters' is the open invitational form ('Come to me, all') of prophetic Wisdom-summons.
